items.prompt: What is a "full table scan"?
choices: Checking every row in a table one by one until a match is found
A specialized index structure built just for fast full-text search
A complete copy of the database kept on a separate disk
A query that stops once it reads the very first matching row found
items.explanation: A full table scan checks every single row in order, looking for a match — its cost grows in direct proportion to the number of rows in the table.

items.prompt: How does a full table scan's cost change as row count grows?
choices: It stays constant regardless of row count
It grows in direct (linear) proportion to row count
It shrinks as row count grows
It grows only if the table has an index
items.explanation: A full scan checks every row, so doubling the row count roughly doubles the number of checks needed — cost grows linearly with data size.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, the login query took 2ms at 500 users and 400ms at 2,000,000 users. What changed about the query itself?
choices: The query itself was quietly rewritten to be less efficient
Nothing about the query changed — only the row count grew
The database engine running underneath it was downgraded
The email column used in the lookup was renamed along the way
items.explanation: The query and code were unchanged — the slowdown came entirely from the table outgrowing the point where a full scan was cheap enough to go unnoticed.

items.prompt: A full table scan checks rows in which order?
choices: Whatever order the rows happen to be physically stored in, not sorted by any column's value
Always sorted ascending by the primary key before any checking begins
Randomly shuffled on every single query execution
Reverse-chronological order, newest row first
items.explanation: A full scan has no shortcut — it walks rows in storage order and checks each one; it isn't using any column's sort order, because without an index there isn't one to use.

items.prompt: Roughly how many rows does a full table scan check in the worst case (no match found) on a table of 1,000 rows?
choices: All 1,000 rows
About 10 rows (log2 of 1,000)
Exactly 1 row
500 rows, half the table
items.explanation: With no match anywhere in the table, a full scan has no way to know that early — it has to check every single row before concluding there's no match.

items.prompt: What is the Big-O cost of a full table scan in terms of row count n?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
items.explanation: A full scan's cost is O(n) — directly proportional to the number of rows, since every row potentially has to be checked.

items.prompt: A table grows from 100,000 to 300,000 rows (3x more rows). Roughly how much more work does a full table scan do?
choices: About 3x more work
About 9x more work
No real change
About 1.5x more work
items.explanation: Full scan cost is directly proportional to row count, so tripling the rows roughly triples the work — that's what "linear" means.

items.prompt: Without any index on `email`, what's the most direct fix for the opening scenario's slow login query, without changing the query text?
choices: Add an index on the email column
Rewrite the query in a different programming language
Delete old user records to shrink the table
Increase the server's screen resolution
items.explanation: Adding an index on email lets the database jump close to the matching row instead of scanning all 2,000,000 rows — the query text doesn't need to change at all.

items.prompt: A table has exactly 0 rows matching a query's WHERE clause. Does a full table scan still have to check every row before concluding there's no match?
choices: Yes — with no shortcut, it has to reach the end of the table to be sure nothing matches
No — it stops as soon as it notices the table is empty of matches, before reading anything
No — it only checks the first and last row, which is always enough to tell
It depends on whether the table has a primary key defined
items.explanation: A full scan has no way to know a value is absent without checking every row — the worst case (no match) requires reading the entire table, same cost as finding a match at the very end.
items.reference:
🔎 Full scan — check row 1, row 2, row 3 ... until a match or the end
📈 Cost — grows linearly: 2x rows ≈ 2x checks

Why: without an index, this is the only way a database can find a row — nothing tells it where to look.
items.reflection: Where else have you seen a process that worked fine at a small scale quietly become the bottleneck purely because of growth, with nothing else about it changing?

No index is ever worth adding until a table exceeds exactly 1,000,000 rows

items.prompt: What is a database index?
choices: A separate structure built ahead of time to make lookups on a column fast without scanning every row
A detailed log file recording, in order, every single query the database has ever executed
A complete backup copy of the table, kept automatically on a totally separate physical disk
A configuration setting that makes every single write to a table complete noticeably faster
items.explanation: An index is a separate, pre-built structure (sorted or hashed) mapping column values to row locations, so a lookup can jump close to the answer instead of scanning every row.

items.prompt: Which trade-off does adding a database index actually make?
choices: It's pure upside — meaningfully faster reads across the board, with no downside whatsoever
It uses extra disk space and slows down writes to the indexed column, in exchange for faster reads
It makes reads measurably slower while making writes to that same column faster instead
It only changes how the table's columns are displayed, never the actual query speed at all
items.explanation: An index needs its own storage, and every insert/update/delete on the indexed column has to update the index too — indexing trades write cost and disk space for read speed, not a free upgrade.

items.prompt: How is a database index similar to a dictionary?
choices: Both store their entries in precisely the order they were each originally entered, unsorted
Both are organized (sorted) specifically to let you find an entry without reading everything before it
Both require memorizing every single entry in the book ahead of time, cover to cover, by heart
Neither one actually has anything meaningful in common with the other at all, really
items.explanation: A dictionary's alphabetical order exists precisely so you can find a word without reading the whole book — an index makes the same trade for a database column.

items.prompt: What does an index actually store for each value, besides the value itself?
choices: A pointer / row location telling the database where to find the full row
A full duplicate copy of every other column in that same row
The exact timestamp of when that row was last read by any query
Nothing else — the index only ever stores the value, with no way back to the row
items.explanation: An index maps a value to a row location (a pointer back to the real row) — it's the map, not a copy of the data itself.

items.prompt: Does an index replace the original table?
choices: No — it's a second, smaller structure alongside the table, pointing back to real rows
Yes — once an index exists, the original table can be safely deleted
Yes, but only for tables under 1,000 rows
An index and a table are two names for the exact same thing
items.explanation: An index is additional structure built on top of the table, not a replacement — the table still holds the actual row data.

items.prompt: Why isn't "index every column on every table" a free win?
choices: Because most databases have a hard limit of exactly one index per table
Because every index costs disk space and slows every write to that column, whether or not it's ever used
Because adding more indexes makes reads measurably slower, in every case
Because columns can only be indexed if they're already marked UNIQUE
items.explanation: Each index is extra storage, and has to be kept up to date on every write to that column — indexing something nobody queries that way is pure ongoing cost with no offsetting benefit.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what's the fix that gets the login query back to fast, without touching the query text?
choices: Adding an index on the email column
Switching the whole database to a different vendor
Caching the entire users table in application memory permanently
Renaming the email column to something shorter
items.explanation: An index on email lets the database jump near the matching row instead of scanning all rows — nothing about the query itself needs to change.

items.prompt: A column is indexed. Does that guarantee every query touching that column will automatically be fast?
choices: Not necessarily — some query patterns can silently bypass an index even though it exists
Yes, always — any query on an indexed column is guaranteed fast, with no exceptions
Only if the table has fewer than 100 rows
Only if the query also includes an ORDER BY clause
items.explanation: An index being present is not the same as an index being usable for every query shape — certain patterns (covered later) can defeat it entirely.

items.prompt: A column is indexed, but a report shows that writes to that table have gotten noticeably slower since the index was added, while reads sped up. Is this surprising, given what an index actually costs?
choices: Yes — an index should never affect write performance in any way
No — every insert/update/delete on the indexed column has to update the index's own structure too, which is the expected cost side of the index's read/write trade-off
Yes — this specifically means the index was built incorrectly and needs to be rebuilt
No, but only because the table in question must have more than 1,000,000 rows
items.explanation: Slower writes alongside faster reads is the index doing exactly what it's supposed to — the maintenance cost on writes is the other half of the trade-off, not a malfunction.
items.reference:
📖 Index — a dictionary's alphabetical order, not the book's chapter order
⚖️ Trade-off — costs disk space + slower writes, buys faster reads

Why: a dictionary lets you find a word without reading the whole book because its entries are pre-sorted — an index makes the same trade for a database column.
items.reflection: Where else in life do you pre-pay a small ongoing maintenance cost (keeping something sorted or organized) specifically so a later lookup is fast?

items.prompt: A table is write-heavy (constant inserts) and almost never read by that particular column. Does adding an index on that rarely-read column make sense?
choices: Yes, indexes should be added to every column regardless of how it's actually used
Probably not — the ongoing write cost of maintaining that index would be paid constantly, for a read benefit that's essentially never used
Yes, because indexes only cost disk space, never write time, so there's no downside
It depends only on how many columns the table has in total
items.explanation: The index's cost (slower writes, extra storage) is paid on every write regardless of whether reads ever use it — indexing should match actual read access patterns, not be applied blindly.

items.prompt: If every row in a table were deleted, would the table's index(es) on it also need to be emptied, or can an index exist independently of the table's actual row contents?
choices: An index is built from and points back to actual rows — deleting all rows means the index has nothing left to point to and is effectively emptied along with the table
Indexes are entirely independent and would keep listing all the old (now-deleted) rows forever, even after the table is empty
Indexes are rebuilt from scratch only once a year, on a fixed schedule, regardless of how much data changes
Deleting rows has no effect on an index at all, under any circumstances
items.explanation: Because an index maps values to row locations in the real table, it has to be kept in sync with the table's actual contents — it can't meaningfully exist pointing at rows that no longer exist.

items.prompt: What makes a B-tree index different from a full table scan?
choices: It deliberately stores rows in a random, unsorted order purely to speed up write operations
It's a balanced, sorted tree structure where lookup cost grows logarithmically, not linearly, with row count
It only ever works correctly on numeric columns, and never on strings, dates, or booleans
It completely removes the need to store the original table's underlying row data at all
items.explanation: A B-tree keeps values sorted in a balanced tree, so a lookup only needs to make a handful of comparisons (roughly log2 of the row count) instead of checking every row.

items.prompt: Roughly how does a B-tree's lookup cost grow as the row count grows?
choices: Logarithmically — doubling the rows adds only about one more comparison
Linearly — doubling the rows always doubles the comparisons needed
Exponentially — doubling the rows squares the comparisons required
It doesn't grow at all, no matter how many rows are added
items.explanation: A B-tree lookup cost is O(log n) — at 2,000,000 rows it takes roughly 21 comparisons, barely more than the ~9 comparisons needed at 500 rows.

items.prompt: Because a B-tree keeps values sorted, which extra capability does it get for free, beyond exact-match lookups?
choices: Range queries and sorted output on the indexed column
The ability to store duplicate rows more efficiently
Automatic deletion of old rows after a fixed time
Faster writes than an unindexed table
items.explanation: Staying sorted means a B-tree can answer "everything between X and Y" or "give me these in order" without extra work — a hash index can't do either.

items.prompt: What is the Big-O cost of a B-tree lookup in terms of row count n?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
items.explanation: A B-tree lookup is O(log n) — the balanced tree structure means each comparison cuts the remaining search space roughly in half.

items.prompt: At 500 rows, a B-tree lookup needs about 9 comparisons. At 2,000,000 rows (4,000x more data), about how many comparisons does it need?
choices: About 21 — barely more, not proportionally more
About 36,000 — scaled proportionally with the row count
Still exactly 9 — logarithmic means literally zero change
About 4,000 — one comparison per 1,000x of growth
items.explanation: Doubling the rows only adds about one more comparison for a B-tree — going from 500 to 2,000,000 rows only moves the comparison count from about 9 to about 21.

items.prompt: Is a B-tree index generally a reasonable default choice for most indexed columns?
choices: Yes — it supports exact match, range queries, and sorted output, covering the most common query needs
No — it's only useful for numeric primary keys
No — it's always slower than a hash index for every kind of query
Yes, but only on tables under 10,000 rows
items.explanation: Because a B-tree supports exact match, ranges, and sorted output all at once, it's the sensible default unless a column's access pattern is purely exact-match (where a hash index may edge it out).

items.prompt: A B-tree lookup walking down the tree is best compared to which everyday action?
choices: Flipping to a random page of a book and hoping to land on the right word
Opening a dictionary near the middle, checking which half the word falls in, and repeating on the smaller half
Reading a book cover to cover, page by page
Memorizing the entire contents of a book before searching it
items.explanation: That halving-and-repeating action is exactly the logarithmic search pattern a B-tree performs — each step discards half of what's left to check.

items.prompt: A table doubles from 1,000,000 to 2,000,000 rows. Roughly how much more work does a B-tree lookup need, versus a full scan on the same growth?
choices: The B-tree barely changes (about 1 more comparison); the full scan's work roughly doubles
Both roughly double
The B-tree's work roughly doubles; the full scan barely changes
Neither changes at all
items.explanation: This is the entire point of the linear-vs-logarithmic contrast: doubling the rows roughly doubles a full scan's work but adds only about one comparison to a B-tree lookup.

items.prompt: A table has exactly 1 row. Roughly how many comparisons would a B-tree lookup need to find it?
choices: Essentially 0–1 — log2(1) is 0, so almost no searching is needed at that trivial scale
Still exactly 9, the same as at 500 rows, because B-trees have a fixed minimum cost
Exactly 1,000,000 comparisons, matching a full scan
It's undefined — B-trees cannot be built on a single-row table
items.explanation: Logarithmic cost shrinks toward zero as n shrinks — at n=1 there's nothing meaningful left to search, which is consistent with log2(1)=0.
items.reference:
🌳 B-tree — balanced, sorted tree
📉 Cost — O(log n): doubling rows adds ~1 comparison, not double the comparisons

Why: because the tree stays sorted, it also answers range queries ("age > 30") for free — a full scan or hash index can't say the same.
items.reflection: Think of another place you've seen a sorted structure (an address book, a filing system) pay off specifically because it lets you discard half the remaining search space at each step.

A hash index — its O(1) lookups make it strictly better for any query shape
Neither can serve both — two separate indexes would always be required
It depends only on whether the column is numeric or text
items.explanation: A B-tree's sort order lets it answer range queries for free in addition to exact match, so one B-tree index can serve both needs — a hash index structurally cannot answer the range half at all.

About 8 more comparisons, matching the 8x row growth directly
About 64 more comparisons (8 squared)
No additional comparisons at all, regardless of growth

items.prompt: What is a hash index best suited for?
choices: Range queries, like finding every row whose value falls between two given bounds
Exact-match lookups, where average-case cost is constant regardless of row count
Sorting an entire table in place by the value of the indexed column
Finding the single row whose value is closest to a given target value
items.explanation: A hash index gives average O(1) exact-match lookups — but hashing destroys value order, so it can't answer range or sorted-output queries at all.

items.prompt: Why can't a hash index answer a range query like "find every row with age between 30 and 40"?
choices: Because hash indexes are inherently and unconditionally slower than B-trees for literally every kind of query imaginable
Because hashing scatters values into unrelated positions, so there's no way to know which values fall between two others without checking every one
Because range queries simply aren't a valid, well-formed kind of query that the SQL language supports at all
Because hash indexes are structurally only ever able to work correctly on string-typed columns, never on numbers
items.explanation: A hash function deliberately scrambles similar inputs into unrelated bucket positions — that's what makes lookups fast, but it also destroys the ordering a range query depends on.

items.prompt: What is the Big-O cost of a hash index's exact-match lookup, on average?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
items.explanation: A hash index computes a bucket from the value's hash and jumps almost directly there — average-case this is O(1), independent of row count.

items.prompt: What kind of column access pattern is a hash index the right fit for?
choices: An opaque token or key that's only ever looked up by exact match, never by range or sort order
A birthdate column that's frequently filtered by "born after year X"
A price column used in ORDER BY price queries
A column that needs to support both ranges and exact match equally well
items.explanation: When range queries and sorted output will genuinely never be needed, a hash index's O(1) average lookup is the better fit — exactly the case for an opaque token with no natural order to exploit.

items.prompt: A hash index scrambles input values into bucket positions. What does this scrambling cost the index, structurally?
choices: The ability to answer range queries or produce sorted output
The ability to perform exact-match lookups at all
The ability to store more than one value per bucket
Nothing — scrambling has no real downside
items.explanation: The scrambling is exactly what makes exact-match lookups fast, but it also destroys the "nearby values are nearby in the index" property that range queries rely on.

items.prompt: Compared to a B-tree, is a hash index generally faster or slower for a pure exact-match lookup?
choices: Generally faster — O(1) average versus O(log n)
Generally slower, because hashing takes extra computation
Always exactly the same speed in every real system
It depends entirely on the number of columns in the table
items.explanation: A hash index's O(1) average lookup is typically faster than a B-tree's O(log n) for pure exact-match lookups — the B-tree's extra capability (ranges, sort order) comes at a small cost the hash index doesn't pay.

items.prompt: Does a hash index keep the indexed values in any meaningful order?
choices: No — hashing scatters values into buckets with no relationship to their original order
Yes — it keeps them in the exact same sorted order a B-tree would
Yes, but only for numeric columns
It depends on how the table's primary key was defined
items.explanation: A hash function's whole purpose is to convert a value into a bucket position with no relationship to nearby values — that's the mechanism, and the reason order is lost.

items.prompt: A session-token cache looks up tokens only by exact match, never by range or sort order. Which index type fits this access pattern best?
choices: A hash index
A B-tree index
No index of any kind would ever help here
A full table scan is always preferable for token lookups
items.explanation: With no range or sort-order need, a hash index's O(1) average exact-match lookup is pure upside — the B-tree's extra sorted-order capability would go unused here.

items.prompt: A hash index on `email` exists. Someone proposes using it to answer `ORDER BY email`. What happens?
choices: It works fine and even speeds up the sort, since the index is already built on email
It can't help — a hash index's bucket order has no relationship to the sorted order the query needs
It silently returns results in a random, meaningless order with no error
The database automatically converts the hash index into a B-tree just for this one query
items.explanation: Sorted output needs values to be stored or retrievable in order — a hash index's bucket placement is unrelated to sort order, so it offers no help for ORDER BY at all; the database would need a different index or an explicit sort step.

Why: the same scrambling that makes lookups fast is what destroys the ordering a range query needs.

Rebuild the hash index with a bigger bucket count, which will enable range support

items.prompt: What does "selectivity" mean for an indexed column?
choices: How much extra disk space the index's internal structure ends up taking up on disk over time
How much the index actually narrows a search — a mostly-unique column is highly selective, a mostly-repeated column is not
Whether or not the column is even allowed to contain NULL values in the first place
How frequently the values stored in that particular column happen to get updated over time
items.explanation: Selectivity measures how much an index narrows the search. A near-unique column like email narrows a lot; a column like a boolean flag with only two values narrows almost nothing.

items.prompt: Why does an index on a boolean column like is_active (true/false) usually help a query very little?
choices: Because boolean columns simply can't be indexed by the database engine at all, under any configuration
Because with only two possible values, the index barely narrows the search — roughly half the table still matches either value
Because boolean indexes always take noticeably longer to build than any other kind of index
Because booleans are actually stored internally as plain text, which breaks indexing entirely
items.explanation: A column with only a couple of distinct values has low selectivity — an index on it still leaves a huge fraction of the table matching, so the database may reasonably prefer a full scan.

items.prompt: Which of these columns is likely the MOST selective (narrows a search the most)?
choices: A unique email address column
A boolean is_active column
A country column with 5 possible values
A status column with 3 possible values
items.explanation: A near-unique column like email narrows a search down to essentially one row — the opposite of a column with only a handful of repeated values.

items.prompt: A column has 1,000,000 rows and only 2 distinct values, split roughly evenly. About what fraction of the table does an index lookup on one of those values still return?
choices: About half the table (500,000 rows)
A single row
About 1% of the table
Zero rows, always
items.explanation: With only 2 roughly even values, matching one value still returns about half the table — that's a low-selectivity column, since the index barely narrows anything.

items.prompt: Is a highly selective column always worth indexing?
choices: Usually yes, if it's actually queried that way — high selectivity means the index narrows the search a lot
No — high selectivity columns should never be indexed
Only if the column is also the primary key
Selectivity has no bearing on whether indexing is worth it

items.prompt: A table grows from 10,000 to 10,000,000 rows (1,000x more data). A full scan's time grows by roughly 1,000x. By roughly what factor should a B-tree lookup's comparison count grow?

items.prompt: Why isn't "just add an index to every column" a good default strategy?
choices: Because most relational databases only ever support a hard maximum of two indexes per table, total
Because every index costs disk space and slows down writes to that column, whether or not it ever gets used by a query
Because adding an index to a column actually makes read queries slower instead of faster, always
Because indexes are automatically deleted by the database engine after exactly 30 days of disuse
items.explanation: Each index is extra storage and has to be updated on every write to that column — indexing a column nobody queries that way trades write performance for a read benefit that's never used.

items.prompt: A table has an index on last_name, but every query filters by last_name AND birth_year together. What's the issue?
choices: There's genuinely no issue at all here — the existing last_name index already fully optimizes this exact combined query on its own
The index on last_name alone doesn't match the actual query pattern — a combined index on (last_name, birth_year) would serve this specific query better
Indexes can only ever be built against a single column at a time, so a query like this one can never be optimized
birth_year should categorically never be referenced inside any WHERE clause, under any circumstances whatsoever
items.explanation: An index should generally match how columns are actually queried together. An index on last_name alone still leaves birth_year filtering unindexed for this query — a composite index on both matches the real access pattern.

items.prompt: What is a composite (multi-column) index best suited for?
choices: Queries that filter or sort on more than one of the indexed columns together, matching the actual combined access pattern
Making every single-column query against the table automatically and uniformly faster, with no other changes needed
Replacing the underlying table's need to have its own dedicated primary key entirely, once it exists
Storing several redundant copies of the exact same table purely for safety and disaster recovery reasons
items.explanation: A composite index is built to match a query pattern that filters on multiple columns together — e.g. (last_name, birth_year) — something a single-column index on either alone doesn't fully serve.

items.prompt: A table has separate single-column indexes on last_name and on birth_year. Every query filters WHERE last_name = ? AND birth_year = ? together. What would likely serve this query pattern better?
choices: A single composite index on (last_name, birth_year) built specifically for that combined lookup
Deleting both of the existing single-column indexes outright, since neither one is genuinely useful
Adding a third, completely unrelated index on the email column instead of fixing the real problem
Nothing at all — two single-column indexes are always functionally equivalent to one composite index
items.explanation: Two separate single-column indexes don't combine into the same thing as one composite index built for the exact (last_name, birth_year) pattern the queries actually use — the composite index is purpose-built for this access pattern.

items.prompt: What does every index cost on each insert, update, or delete touching its column?
choices: The index's own internal structure has to be updated to stay consistent with the new data
Nothing at all — indexes are entirely separate from write operations
The entire table has to be rebuilt from scratch
Only reads are affected; writes are always unaffected by indexes
items.explanation: Keeping an index accurate means updating it alongside every write to its column — this is the ongoing cost side of the read/write trade-off every index makes.

items.prompt: A table is indexed on 15 different columns, most of which are rarely or never used in any WHERE clause. What's the likely consequence?
choices: Writes to the table are paying the maintenance cost of 15 indexes, most of which provide no offsetting read benefit
Reads will automatically become 15 times faster across the board
Nothing changes; unused indexes have zero cost of any kind
The table will be unable to accept any further writes once it reaches 15 indexes
items.explanation: Every one of those 15 indexes has to be kept up to date on every relevant write, regardless of whether it's ever actually used by a query — that's pure ongoing cost for the unused ones.

items.prompt: What's the right way to decide which columns to index, according to this unit?

Index every column in every table by default, with no exceptions
Only index columns whose name contains the word "id"
Index columns in the exact order they appear in the table's schema definition
items.explanation: The right call is matching indexes to real access patterns — a column being conceptually important doesn't mean it's queried in a way that benefits from an index.

items.prompt: Does adding an index ever genuinely have zero cost?
choices: No — it always costs at least some disk space and some write-time maintenance, even if that cost is small relative to the read benefit
Yes, as long as the column being indexed is never updated after the table is created
Yes, for any column with fewer than 100 distinct values
Yes, indexes on primary keys are always free with no exceptions
items.explanation: Every index has some non-zero storage and write-maintenance cost — the question is always whether the read benefit is worth paying that cost, not whether the cost exists at all.

items.prompt: A table has a composite index on (last_name, birth_year). A query filters `WHERE birth_year = ?` alone, without last_name. Can this composite index help that query as effectively as a dedicated index on birth_year alone would?
choices: Generally not as effectively — a composite index's usefulness typically depends on filtering from its leading column(s) first; filtering only on a later column in the composite often can't use it the same way a dedicated single-column index would
Yes — a composite index on any set of columns is always exactly as useful for a query on any subset or single one of those columns
Yes, but only if birth_year happens to be listed first in the composite index definition
No index of any kind, composite or single-column, can ever help a query filtering on just one column
items.explanation: Composite indexes are generally most useful when the query's filter conditions align with the index's column order starting from the front — a query that skips the leading column often can't take advantage of a composite index the way it could a dedicated index built for that specific column.

items.prompt: Implement `midpointIndex(lo, hi)` — return the midpoint index between lo and hi (inclusive), the way binary search picks which element to check next. Use integer division (no fractional results).
items.explanation: The midpoint is what binary search checks at each step — using `>> 1` (or Math.floor division) keeps the result an integer index, rounding down when lo+hi is odd.

items.prompt: Implement `compareValues(a, b)` — return -1 if a < b, 1 if a > b, 0 if equal. This is the comparison binary search uses at each step to decide which half to keep.
items.explanation: This three-way comparison is exactly what decides, at each step of binary search, whether to keep searching the left half, the right half, or stop because a match was found.

items.prompt: Implement `worstCaseComparisons(n)` — return the worst-case number of comparisons a binary search needs over n sorted items, i.e. `Math.ceil(Math.log2(n))` for n >= 1 (return 0 for n <= 1).
items.explanation: This reproduces L2's exact worst-case comparison chart — the formula is the whole reason B-tree lookup cost is called O(log n): the comparisons needed grow with the logarithm of the row count, not the row count itself.

items.prompt: Implement `isSortedAscending(arr)` — return true if every element is less than or equal to the one after it, false otherwise. An empty array or single-element array counts as sorted.
items.explanation: Binary search only works correctly on data that's actually sorted — this check is the precondition every binary search implementation silently relies on.

items.prompt: Implement `windowSize(lo, hi)` — return how many elements remain to be searched between lo and hi inclusive (i.e. `hi - lo + 1`).
items.explanation: Tracking how much of the search space remains makes the halving visible — this quantity should roughly halve on every step of a correct binary search, which is the mechanical reason the comparison count grows logarithmically.

items.prompt: Implement `narrowLeft(hi, mid)` — given that the target is smaller than the value at `mid`, return the new `hi` boundary to search next (the element just before mid).
items.explanation: Once the midpoint is ruled out as too large, the next search window drops everything from mid onward — this one-line update is what actually halves the remaining range on each step.

items.prompt: Implement `narrowRight(lo, mid)` — given that the target is larger than the value at `mid`, return the new `lo` boundary to search next (the element just after mid).
items.explanation: This is the mirror image of narrowing left — when the target is bigger than the midpoint's value, the entire left half (including mid) is ruled out in one step.

items.prompt: Implement `foundAt(sortedArr, mid, target)` — return true if the element at index `mid` equals `target`, false otherwise.
items.explanation: This is the stopping condition binary search checks at every step before deciding to narrow left or right — simple on its own, but it's what ends the search the moment a match lands exactly on the current midpoint.

items.prompt: Implement `isWithinRange(value, from, to)` — return true if `from <= value <= to`, false otherwise.
items.explanation: This is the exact condition a range query is really asking for every row — a sorted index answers it efficiently by skipping straight to the boundary instead of checking this condition against every single row.

items.explanation: This is the ending boundary of a range — pairing a lower bound and an upper bound like this is exactly how a range query knows where to stop collecting rows.

items.prompt: L3's benchmark shows the full scan slowed down about 6,200x while the binary search only slowed down about 7x, when going from 500 to 2,000,000 rows. What does this demonstrate?
choices: That binary search is fundamentally and rather unexpectedly broken once row counts get sufficiently large for any real workload
That linear-cost operations (full scan) degrade roughly proportional to data growth, while logarithmic-cost operations (binary search / B-tree) barely degrade at all
That the benchmark's underlying measurements are simply unreliable and shouldn't be trusted at all, in general, by anyone
That 2,000,000 rows is just categorically too many for any real production database to ever realistically handle correctly
items.explanation: This is the practical, measured version of the O(n) vs. O(log n) difference: a 4,000x data increase means roughly 4,000x more full-scan work (plus real hardware effects like cache misses push it even higher), but the binary search barely notices.

items.prompt: L3 notes that the full scan's real slowdown (~6,200x) was higher than the row-count increase (4,000x). What's the most likely explanation given the unit's own framing?
choices: The benchmark code itself most likely contains a subtle bug that artificially inflates only the full-scan timing
Real hardware effects like cache misses on a much larger array push a linear-cost operation's actual slowdown past a perfectly proportional increase
JavaScript arrays become slower than their theoretical complexity suggests as they grow, invalidating Big-O reasoning entirely
The 2,000,000-row benchmark run most likely used a completely different, faster CPU than the 500-row run did
items.explanation: Big-O describes the shape of growth, not the exact constant factor — real-world costs like cache misses on a much larger array can make an O(n) operation's actual slowdown exceed the row-count ratio itself, while the underlying linear relationship still holds.

items.prompt: True or false: a sub-linear growth rate (like O(log n) or O(1)) means a strategy's measured time literally never changes at all as row count grows.
choices: False — sub-linear means it grows much more slowly than the input, not that it's perfectly flat; small real increases (extra comparisons, Map resizing) are still expected

items.explanation: Sub-linear growth is about the relative SHAPE of the curve, not a promise of zero change — a binary search doing a few more comparisons, or a Map needing to resize internally, are both small real costs consistent with still being O(log n) or O(1) average.
